newsitem.title: USA: USDA cotton crop data seen bullish for futures.
newsitem.headline: USDA cotton crop data seen bullish for futures.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department's September cotton crop production estimates, released Wednesday, are bullish for the cotton market, analysts said.
"The number was certainly bullish," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "The report is going to encourage a strong open, maybe 1.50 to 2.00 (cents a lb) higher."
USDA pegged 1996/97 crop production at 17.900 million 480-lb bales, down from 18.577 million bales estimated last month.
"It catches everyone off guard," said Smith Barney vice president David Brandon Jr. "The market will probably open up sharply."
Brandon said in the near term the market may move up into the mid-to-upper 70s. NYCE most-active December cotton settled Tuesday at 73.07 cents a lb, up 0.22 cent.

Most analysts had expected today's estimate to come in between 18.3 million and 18.8 million bales, with most projections at the high of the range after beneficial rains in Texas and the Southeastern U.S. in the past month were expected to result in higher crop yields.
But USDA said high temperatures in California and dryness in Louisiana and Arkansas cut into the cotton production estimate.
"We are surprised by the big decrease in three key states," said Frank Schneider and Co Inc analyst Sharon Johnson. "It was very much in conflict with what we were hearing in yields."
But Johnson said she was also surprised USDA did not cut demand more, with U.S. cotton's steep price compared to the rest of the world.
USDA estimated U.S. exports fell to 6.2 million bales versus August's 6.6 million bales. Meanwhile, domestic use was raised to 11.2 million bales from 11.0 million bales last month.
U.S. 1996/97 ending stocks were pegged at 3.6 million bales, compared to 4.0 million bales last month.
"We're not selling any cotton as it is, it adds insult to injury," Johnson said. She expects ending stocks will rise again to over 4.0 millions bales.
Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes agreed the problem is on the demand side.
"We might see an initial bullish response to the report," Ganes said. "But we still have a bearish scenario."
